extracted.intended_audience: general readers, game developers, and legal practitioners interested in video game copyright/cloning cases
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a videogame clone infringes copyright or trade dress by distinguishing unprotectable ideas and functional elements from protectable expressive elements (the game's 'look and feel') and applying tests for substantial similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction–Filtration–Comparison (AFC) test for substantial similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-step test applied to determine if alleged copying amounts to copyright infringement: abstract the work, filter out unprotectable elements, then compare the remaining expressive elements for substantial similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied as in Computer Associates v. Altai and Nichols v. Universal Pictures; Wolfson instructed courts to compare 'as they would appear to a layman [by] concentrating upon the gross features rather than an examination of minutiae'. The court should filter out ideas, scènes à faire, functional elements, and then compare remaining expression; if one 'has to squint to find distinctions only at a granular level, then the works are likely to be substantially similar.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea–expression distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects expression, not general ideas, methods, or systems; game mechanics and rules are generally considered ideas and not copyrightable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the Copyright Office advises: 'copyright does not protect the idea for a game, its name or title, or the method or methods for playing it.' This guides filtration of unprotectable elements in AFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scènes à faire (stock/common elements exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock scenes and generic details common among creative works are not protected by copyright and should be filtered out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat commonly used or inevitable elements as unprotectable scènes à faire; a defendant may argue that similarities arise from such stock elements rather than protected expression. Wolfson considered and rejected scènes à faire arguments for Tetris because the game was found to be uniquely expressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merger doctrine (when expression merges with idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an idea can be expressed in only a limited number of ways, the expression 'merges' with the idea and is ineligible for copyright protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may claim merger to avoid protection for certain elements; Judge Wolfson rejected a merger claim regarding Tetris block art, finding those details were not essential or inseparable from the game's ideas, rules, or functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-copyrightable gameplay mechanics and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental game mechanics—e.g., vertically falling blocks, player rotation, forming lines to score points, and losing when blocks reach the top—are treated as ideas or methods and are not copyrightable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolfson explicitly ruled that the gameplay of Tetris (falling/rotating blocks, line-clearing/scoring, losing condition) is not subject to copyright protection; these should be filtered out in AFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyrightable expressive elements (specific audiovisual/interface elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific visual/audio/interface elements and their particular selection/arrangement can be protected as expression (examples identified by the court include: the twenty-by-ten square game board, display of randomized junk blocks at start, a block's 'shadow' showing where it will land, display of the next piece to fall, blocks changing color when they land, and the board filling up when the game is over).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying one such expressive element in isolation may not prove infringement, but copying multiple such elements (or the combination/arrangement) can support a finding of substantial similarity and infringement, as it may show replication of the game's 'look and feel.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Look-and-feel / side-by-side gross-features comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate similarity by viewing the works side-by-side and concentrating on gross, layman-perceptible features rather than minutiae; the court compares overall look and feel to assess substantial similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolfson's directive: compare 'as they would appear to a layman' and if distinctions require squinting at granular details, the works are likely substantially similar. This emphasizes an ordinary-observer perspective in addition to analytical filtering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade dress / likelihood of consumer confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual presentation and marketing style can constitute trade dress, and use of the same color and style in marketing can create a likelihood of consumer confusion supporting trade dress infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolfson examined Mino's marketing materials and found that use of the same color and piece style created a likelihood of confusion; marketing/packaging and promotional materials are therefore relevant evidence in trade dress claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality doctrine (functional elements are unprotectable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are functional—i.e., essential to how a game operates or to its utilitarian purpose—are not protected by copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts filter out functional elements in AFC; however the specific selection or arrangement of standard devices (non-functional expressive choices) may still be protected as expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection or arrangement of standard devices as protectable expression
rubrics_metrics.description: While individual standard game devices may be generic, a particular selection or arrangement of those devices can constitute a unique expression eligible for copyright protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and the court noted that a 'specific selection or arrangement' of standard game devices may qualify as unique expression; this supports protection beyond isolated mechanics if the combination is original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of copying and intent (admissions, direct copying, licensing attempts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct admissions of copying, evidence that a developer copied assets from the plaintiff's product, attempts to license and subsequent refusal, and marketing representations are evidentiary factors relevant to infringement determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Xio, the founder admitted copying Mino directly from the official Tetris app and had sought a license; such facts can bolster an infringement claim and the inference that similarities are not coincidental or independently developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific, narrow standard — case-by-case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome of look-and-feel and clone disputes is highly fact-specific and narrow; courts apply a fact-heavy analysis and results may be difficult to predict outside of the particular circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators caution that the Tetris ruling creates a 'narrow, fact-heavy legal standard' and that courts have applied the standard carefully, meaning practitioners should expect case-specific litigation rather than bright-line rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of graphical user interface (GUI) and audiovisual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may treat a game's graphical user interface and audiovisual presentation as protectable in the same manner as audiovisual works, making GUI elements subject to copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tomasz Grzegorczyk and others note the decision recognizes that 'graphic user interface of the game is subject to protection under copyright in the same manner as audiovisual works'; thus GUI design and audiovisual presentation are relevant expressive elements.
